exploration.title: Light Bending Studio
exploration.subject: Physics
exploration.summary: Compare reflection and refraction, then find when a higher-index material keeps a ray inside.
exploration.question: How do angle and travel direction change a ray at a boundary?
exploration.explanation: Reflection stays in the first medium and leaves at the incident angle. Refraction crosses the boundary; Snell’s law relates both angles to the materials’ refractive indices. Refractive index compares light’s speed in vacuum with its speed in a material, so a higher index means slower light. Measure every angle from the normal, the line perpendicular to the boundary. Entering a higher index bends a slanting ray toward the normal; entering a lower index bends it away. Above the critical angle, a higher-to-lower-index ray undergoes total internal reflection.

experiments.title: Cross the critical angle
experiments.instruction: Keep glass to air fixed. Predict whether a transmitted ray remains when only the incident angle changes from 40° to 43°.
experiments.observe: Compare the 40° transmitted ray with its absence at 43°. Relate the change to the 41.8° critical angle.

experiments.title: Reverse the boundary
experiments.instruction: Keep the incident angle at 30°. Predict how the refracted ray changes between air to glass and glass to air.
experiments.observe: Compare the 19.5° and 48.6° refracted angles while the reflected angle remains 30°. Explain toward-versus-away bending.

exploration.misconception: A ray does not totally reflect merely because it meets a boundary. Total internal reflection requires travel from higher to lower refractive index and an incident angle above that pair’s critical angle.
